Rule of thumb: If your vehicle is worth less than £5,000, a used engine may be your only economical option. If you're keeping a £5,000-£15,000 car for 2+ years, the reconditioned premium buys warranty, reliability, and resale value.

ordered.title: What independent garages know
ordered.description: Many UK buyers assume a "used engine" is the cheapest sensible option. In practice, used engines are removed from accident-damaged or scrapped vehicles, rarely inspected internally beyond basic compression testing, sold with unknown maintenance history, and often already near end-of-life on critical components (timing chains, turbos, injectors).

blocks.text: [EM-OBSERVED] "Many UK garages use 'reconditioned' and 'rebuilt' interchangeably to mean a used engine that has been fully stripped, cleaned, inspected, repaired and rebuilt to meet specific performance standards. A reconditioned engine typically undergoes a full technical restoration process that delivers up to 94% of the performance of a brand-new unit - at 40-60% less cost."

✔ You plan to sell within 12 months - no need to invest in long-term reliability
✔ You need the absolute cheapest option - used engines are the lowest upfront cost
✔ Vehicle is being repaired purely to keep mobile
✔ Failure is catastrophic and vehicle is not economically repairable otherwise
✔ Vehicle is worth £5,000-£15,000 - the £600-£1,000 premium buys warranty, reliability, and resale value protection
✔ You plan to keep the car 2+ years - long-term ownership justifies the investment
✔ You want warranty protection beyond 12 months - reconditioned engines typically include 12-24 month full coverage
✔ You want reduced risk of repeat engine failure - all wear components are replaced
✔ Vehicle has high mileage (100k+) but is otherwise in good condition - reconditioning restores the engine to near-new condition

ordered.title: Common questions about used vs reconditioned engines

blocks.question: What's the real difference between used and reconditioned- +
blocks.answer: A used engine is removed from a donor vehicle and sold "as-is" with minimal inspection and a short warranty (1-6 months). A reconditioned engine is fully stripped, cleaned, rebuilt with new wear components (bearings, piston rings, gaskets, timing components), tested, and supplied with 6-24 months warranty. The reconditioned premium (£600-£1,000) buys reliability and peace of mind.

blocks.question: How much does a used engine cost fitted- +
blocks.answer: Used engine fitted costs range from £1,000 to £4,000 depending on engine type and labour rates. Supply-only costs are £500-£1,500. Fitting adds £500-£2,500. See the price breakdown table above for specific engine types.

blocks.question: How much does a reconditioned engine cost fitted- +
blocks.answer: Reconditioned engine fitted costs range from £1,800 to £4,500 for 4-cylinder engines, up to £7,500-£12,000 for V8 performance engines. Supply-only costs are £1,200-£3,500 for 4-cylinder, up to £6,000-£10,000 for V8. Fitting adds £800-£2,500 depending on engine type and region.

blocks.question: Is a reconditioned engine as good as new- +
blocks.answer: A reconditioned engine delivers up to 94% of the performance of a brand-new unit [EM-OBSERVED] at 40-60% less cost. While it may not have every single brand-new component, all wear parts are replaced and the engine is tested to factory tolerances. For most owners, the difference is imperceptible.

blocks.question: What warranty do I get with each option- +
blocks.answer: Used: 1-6 months limited parts-only warranty. Reconditioned: 6-24 months parts + labour warranty. Always check the supplier's warranty terms in writing. Engines Market does not provide warranties - we connect you with suppliers who do.

blocks.question: Should I choose used or reconditioned for my car- +
blocks.answer: If your vehicle is worth under £5,000 , a used engine may be the only economical option. If your vehicle is worth £5,000-£15,000 and you plan to keep it for 2+ years, the reconditioned premium (£600-£1,000) buys warranty, reliability, and resale value protection. See the decision framework above for detailed rules.

blocks.question: What's the risk of buying a used engine- +
blocks.answer: Used engines come with significant hidden risks: timing chain wear (£650-£2,500), turbo degradation (£800-£2,500), oil starvation history (£1,500-£5,000+), injector wear (£300-£1,500), DPF condition (£400-£1,200), and water pump condition (£400-£800). These are all addressed during reconditioning. See the risk analysis section above.

blocks.question: Can I fit a used engine from a different vehicle- +
blocks.answer: Yes, but you need the exact same engine code and often the same variant to ensure compatibility. Your supplier will match the engine code to your vehicle's VIN. Never assume a similar engine will fit.

blocks.question: How long does engine replacement take- +
blocks.answer: From quote request to completion, the average is 5.2 days [EM-VERIFIED]. Used engines typically take 3-5 days; reconditioned engines take 3-7 days due to the additional rebuild and testing process.

blocks.question: What does a reconditioning process actually include- +
blocks.answer: A full reconditioning includes: block cleaning and inspection, crank regrinding if required, new bearings, new or reconditioned pistons and rings, new gaskets and seals, new timing chain and tensioner, oil pump inspection, injector testing and cleaning, turbo inspection, and hot + cold dynamic testing. See the OEM & technical authority section above for full details.

blocks.question: Is it cheaper to repair or replace an engine- +
blocks.answer: If damage is isolated (timing chain rattle caught early, head gasket seepage), targeted repair may be cheaper. Advanced failure (rod knock, snapped timing belt on interference engine) often makes replacement more cost-effective. → Repair vs Replacement comparison

blocks.question: Do I need to tell my insurer about an engine replacement- +
blocks.answer: Yes. Any major mechanical change, including an engine replacement, must be declared to your insurer. Failure to do so could invalidate your insurance. The new engine code and number should be recorded on your V5C (logbook) and insurance policy.
